subject: Cognitive Science
title: Fast and Frugal Heuristics
description: A short lesson to help you apply Fast and Frugal Heuristics.

hook.text: A doctor in the ER has seconds to decide: is this chest pain a heart attack? They don't run a full analysis.

buildup.text: Gerd Gigerenzer showed that simple decision trees—check one cue, then decide—often beat complex models.

discovery.text: These are fast-and-frugal heuristics: rules that use minimal information and still get it right most of the time.

twist.text: In unpredictable environments, simple rules outperform algorithms because they don't overfit noisy data.

climax.text: Evolution designed our brains for good-enough speed, not perfect accuracy. And it works.

punchline.text: Simple rules often beat complex models.

quiz.question: When do fast-and-frugal heuristics perform best?

details.summary: Gigerenzer's research program shows that simple heuristics using minimal information often match or beat complex statistical models. Take-the-best uses a single cue; tallying counts positive features without weighting.
details.whyItMatters: Fast and frugal heuristics challenge the bias-focused narrative. Simple rules are not always inferior to complex analysis; often they are better adapted to uncertain environments.
takeaways: Simple heuristics can match complex models in prediction
Less information and simpler rules reduce overfitting
Environmental structure determines which heuristic works best

faq.question: What is the take-the-best heuristic?
faq.answer: Take-the-best searches through cues in order of validity and stops at the first cue that discriminates between options. If one city has a university and the other does not, choose it as larger and stop looking. This outperforms multiple regression in many real-world prediction tasks.

faq.question: Why can simple heuristics outperform complex models?
faq.answer: Complex models fit noise in the training data, a problem called overfitting. Simple heuristics ignore noise by using fewer cues. In uncertain environments with limited data, this robustness gives simple heuristics a prediction advantage. Less can genuinely be more.
